title: The foldable isn't the future of the phone — it's a two-in-one for a subset of people
dek: Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the bar phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.
why: A solo episode with a product manager's eye that lays out the real experience of using a foldable, the business logic behind Apple entering, and the judgment that phone form factors will diverge rather than converge. Medium information density; the back half is worth more than the front half.
who: Consumers on the fence about buying a foldable, product managers working on hardware and phone products, and anyone following Apple's product strategy and where phone form factors are heading.
skip: You can fast-forward the personal history and position-setting from 0:00 to 5:10; start listening from the shipment data at 12:17.

points.h: The foldable's home turf is China and nowhere else
points.body: In 2025, China's full-year foldable shipments broke ten million units, with Huawei taking 70% — a crushing share. But globally, China is the largest single market, accounting for more than 40% of shipments. In other words, this category isn't evenly distributed the way other phone form factors are; its core users are Chinese bosses holding Huawei foldables in first class and at social occasions. On the broad market, foldables are only 2.5% of global phone shipments, and only 15% of Huawei's own phone shipments.

points.h: The inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time
points.body: Liu Fei used foldables as his daily driver for the better part of a month, and in the end he didn't want to keep them. The biggest problem wasn't the crease, the camera, or the battery — it was the scenario. The inner screen doesn't get opened much: it's unstable one-handed and prone to shaking, and it's more for two-handed use, but in that scenario he'd already be carrying a 10-inch iPad. A Vivo vice president said at a launch event that foldables keep getting better, but the core way you use them is no different from seven years ago, and many users open the inner screen less than 30% of the time. His analogy: it's like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

points.h: Once it gets wider, scrolling feeds actually gets worse
points.body: To accommodate the outer screen, wide-format foldables like the Huawei Pure X Max and the Apple iPhone Door got wider, and scrolling feeds on them is terrible. Xiaohongshu is fine, because it's been adapted; but scrolling Meituan to filter restaurants or Taobao to filter shops, the information that fits on each screen suddenly shrinks. This isn't purely an adaptation problem, it's an aspect-ratio problem: list feeds run vertically, so widening gains you nothing, and the height shrinks, so you see less at once. His impression was that ordering takeout on Meituan, he could only see three restaurants at a time.

points.h: 76% more area, yet widescreen video looks smaller
points.body: A large foldable is nearly square when unfolded, which is a disaster for video and photos. By screen area, opening the inner screen adds 76%, close to double; but if you're watching a widescreen movie, the foldable's inner screen actually loses about 10% of its effective area, because it can't fit the frame. 16:9 content does get bigger, but only by 20%, which is fairly limited. Wide-format foldables have more sensible dimensions and higher effective area, but a 16:10 wide foldable playing 16:9 video still leaves about 10% black bars top and bottom. The point isn't that area naturally increases — it's what you actually want to do with the inner screen.

points.h: Who the two-in-one is a plus for
points.body: Liu Fei says the most important decision logic for whether to buy a foldable is: does it add to or subtract from your existing experience? He has a full set of devices himself — a Windows PC for gaming, a MacBook for work, an iPad for shows — so a foldable is pointless for him. But for many young people, the phone is their only computing device, and a lot of work happens on the phone, offline, so a bigger screen makes the experience much better. Salespeople who travel constantly and need to present a deck to a client in a café get a much better result from the inner screen than the outer one. Flip it around: what you're buying isn't a bar phone that turns into a tablet, it's a foldable iPad mini.

Liu Fei says the Apple Watch and AirPods developed during Cook's tenure are both world-changing products, and AirPods especially so: without AirPods ushering in the era of Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones, you could say there'd be no podcast market, and especially no Chinese podcast market. Chinese podcasting took off in lockstep with Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones — because with noise cancelling, you can actually hear what people are saying while commuting, working out, or doing chores. Before that, those scenarios were usually for listening to music, or to content with very low information density.

points.h: Apple's kill shot is migrating the iPad ecosystem
points.body: The iPhone Door doesn't have such an exaggerated hardware advantage; it uses materials from mature supply chains, weighs 254 grams, and doesn't feel dramatically different from Android flagship foldables. The core advantage is that Apple has the iPad: since the iPad launched in 2010, the 4:3 ratio has accumulated a huge content ecosystem, and a lot of software was already optimised well enough for that ratio before foldable phones even existed, so it can be ported straight to the iPhone Door. For Android, that's a crushing level of ecosystem migration. Apple also did a lot of work on one-handed interaction, putting frequently used buttons on the dominant-hand side — that's a system-level design, and it's relatively easy for developers to follow and adapt to.

points.h: How you define success decides whether it succeeds
points.body: Whether the iPhone Door succeeds depends on how you define success. If you define it as replacing the bar phone, it's nearly impossible; if you define it as becoming a product line that keeps selling, it's very possible. A few million units in the first generation is no problem, and it might even reach ten million; JD reservations have already passed 500,000. Liu Fei says phone form factors won't converge, they'll diverge: the bar phone is the one form factor the whole world would vote for, but other form factors will keep existing and keep differentiating, at every price and in every shape. Foldables won't replace bar phones, even if performance, experience and price were exactly the same, because a substantial number of people simply have no need to open the inner screen.

quotes.text: Once it solves the crease problem, solves the problem of folding-use quality, solves the price problem, maybe it really can become mainstream.

It's a bit like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

By screen area, opening the inner screen adds 76% directly, which feels great, close to double — but if you're watching a widescreen movie, the foldable's inner screen is actually smaller, because it can't fit the frame, and the effective area drops by about 10%.
What you're buying isn't a cardboard phone that turns into a tablet, it's a foldable iPad mini.
Without AirPods ushering in the era of Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones, you could say there'd be no podcast market, and especially no Chinese podcast market.

My judgment is that even if it fully matches the bar phone's performance, experience and every other dimension, and the price is the same, it will still be very hard to replace the bar phone, because a substantial number of people simply have no need to open the inner screen.
